title: Cisco Isovalent Shell and Package Tool Execution in Containers
exclusions: Covers one Isovalent event type. Risk-framework drill-downs that mention Isovalent are a different search.
evidence: Daily counts of the matching events for 30 days, with the pod and binary columns from the search.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Run the test action described in the validation step inside a non-production pod. The next search shows that pod and binary.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Stop the Isovalent HEC export. The search returns no rows for the following hour.

dataSources: `index=containers sourcetype=cisco:isovalent:processExec` from the Cisco Security Cloud (7404) Isovalent input over HEC. Field names are the ones Splunk Security Content lists for this sourcetype: process_exec.process.binary, pod_name, pod_namespace, cluster_name.
spl:
index=containers sourcetype="cisco:isovalent:processExec" earliest=-24h
| where match('process_exec.process.binary', "(?i)/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|curl|wget|nc|ncat|python|python3|perl|apk|apt|apt-get|yum|dnf)$")
| stats count as execs by cluster_name, pod_namespace, pod_name, process_exec.process.binary
| sort - execs
description: Lists containers that started a shell, a downloader, or a package manager. The binary path is process_exec.process.binary, the pod is pod_name and pod_namespace, and the cluster is cluster_name, which are fields Splunk Security Content documents for cisco:isovalent:processExec.
value: Shells and package tools inside a production container are how an attacker explores a cluster after a foothold. This list puts those process starts, with the pod that ran them, in front of the team that owns the namespace.
implementation: Enable the Isovalent HEC input in Cisco Security Cloud into index=containers. Schedule this search hourly.
visualization: Table of the stats output, sorted by the count column, plus a timechart of the count.

references.title: Cisco Security Cloud App for Splunk User Guide

knownFalsePositives:
1. **Health probes and package caches** — kube-system DaemonSets run shells and connect to the API server. Exclude `pod_namespace=kube-system` once you have confirmed those pods.

**Suppression:** exclude the namespaces your platform team owns.
detailedImplementation:
Prerequisites
• Cisco Security Cloud (`CiscoSecurityCloud`, Splunkbase 7404) on the search heads and on the heavy forwarder that exposes the HEC token.
• Isovalent Runtime Security (Tetragon) sending process events to the Splunk integration, and a HEC token scoped to index=containers.
• A role with srchIndexesAllowed on index=containers.

Step 1 — Configure data collection
• In Cisco Security Cloud open the Isovalent card and create the HEC input. The add-on writes `cisco:isovalent:processExec`.
• Confirm fields: `index=containers sourcetype="cisco:isovalent:processExec" | fieldsummary process_exec.process.binary`.

Step 2 — Create the search
```spl
index=containers sourcetype="cisco:isovalent:processExec" earliest=-24h
| where match('process_exec.process.binary', "(?i)/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|curl|wget|nc|ncat|python|python3|perl|apk|apt|apt-get|yum|dnf)$")
| stats count as execs by cluster_name, pod_namespace, pod_name, process_exec.process.binary
| sort - execs
```

Understanding this SPL
• The where clause keeps binaries whose path ends in a shell, a downloader, or a package manager. Those names are the process_exec.process.binary values Tetragon records.
• Arguments are available as process_exec.process.arguments and can be added to the table when an investigation needs the command line.

Step 3 — Validate
• In a non-production namespace, run the action this search looks for and confirm the pod name appears.
• Compare the pod name with `kubectl get pods -A` so a deleted pod is not investigated as live.

• Confirm in the vendor console that the same hour shows the same kind of event before trusting a zero or a spike.

Step 4 — Operationalize
• Hourly search, table on the container-security dashboard.
• Alert on counts above an agreed baseline per namespace, throttled on pod_namespace for 1 hour.

Step 5 — Troubleshooting
• No events: the HEC token or the Isovalent export URL is wrong. The user guide also notes an Edge Processor variant that is alpha; this page uses the HEC input.
• Events exist but the fields are empty: the sourcetype is not `cisco:isovalent:processExec`. Splunk Security Content documents this casing, not an all-lowercase name.
• No data for this sourcetype, with an input error in the Cisco Security Cloud log, means the credential or token is incorrect.
grandmaExplanation: We list containers that started a shell or a package tool, so unexpected activity inside a running application is visible.
